newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish PM says Haughey conduct unacceptable.
newsitem.headline: Irish PM says Haughey conduct unacceptable.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern said on Wednesday that he was "deeply unhappy" that his mentor and predecessor, Charlie Haughey, had misled a tribunal over a million pounds in gifts from a department store tycoon.

"I am deeply unhappy with what I heard from yesterday. I'm afraid it revealed standards of conduct that are unacceptable from one of the most capable leaders this country has seen." Ahern told state broadcaster RTE.
It was Ahern's first comment on Haughey's admission on Tuesday that he misled an official tribunal investigating payments to politicians by businessman Ben Dunne.
Haughey said he received 1.3 million Irish pounds ($2.0 million) from Dunne between 1989 and 1992, the last of the three periods in which he was prime minister.

Ahern, like Haughey, a member of the Fianna Fail party, said he would await the findings of the tribunal before deciding whether further inquiry was needed into allegations of corruption in the political establishment.

"My government is committed to implementing the (tribunal) findings and if there are other matters which the body politic believe require investigating, if the truthfulness and integrity don't add up any more, then they'll have to be further investigated," he said.

Ahern was responding to opposition calls for an investigation into Haughey, a former accountant whose lifestyle included a north Dublin mansion, a private island, a yacht, a stud farm and a fabled wine cellar.
Pressed on whether he would authorise such a probe, Ahern said: "As far as I am concerned, if there are matters that have remained unanswered...then I will certainly do that."
Haughey told the tribunal that Dunne had not asked for political favours, while Dunne told the panel that he gave Haughey cash because the prime miniser was in serious financial difficulty.

Haughey said his financial affairs were entirely in the hands of a former partner in his accountancy firm, Des Traynor, and he was unaware that the money had been paid into his account. Traynor is now dead.
He also denied any recollection that Dunne personally gave him three cheques totalling 210,000 pounds made out to third parties at his private home.
The tribunal was set up after former transport minister Michael Lowry admitted media reports that Dunne had paid for the quarter million pound rennovation of his private home.

The tribunal heard evidence that all political parties had received cash from Dunne for election campaign expenses but Haughey denied being the former Fianna Fail minister said by press reports to have been given 1.3 million pounds.
Political sources noted that Haughey, said by associates to be a ruthless and autocratic leader of both the country and Fianna Fail, groomed Ahern for eventual leadership.
Opposition parties are pressing for a wider probe amid calls for a new code of conduct governing links between big business and the political establishment.
Dunne was dropped by his family five years ago from control of the Dunnes Stores department chain whose green-fronted supermarkets feature in almost all Irish towns.
